summary:
NASA displays vital Earth climate data through colorful visual maps, but relying strictly on sight completely excludes blind and low-vision individuals.

Birla Blitz solves this by converting NASA’s satellite images into sound. When a satellite image is uploaded to a laptop, our tool scans the pixels and turns the data into a short sound chirp played through the speaker. Across the room, our lightweight Android app hears this chirp through its microphone—with zero Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or cables needed.

How It Helps Blind and Low-Vision People:
Instead of needing to see colors on a screen, the phone vibrates and automatically reads the entire scientific explanation out loud using its built-in voice. It clearly describes what the colors mean—such as freezing polar temperatures versus dangerous desert heatwaves.

Key Benefits:
Inclusive Accessibility: Translates sight into spoken words so visually impaired users can easily understand complex Earth science.
100% Offline & Disaster-Proof: Continues working during cyclones and floods even when local cell towers and internet cables fail.
Zero Cost & Fast: Uses the phone’s native speech engine instead of expensive cloud AI subscriptions, providing instant speech at zero cost.
details:
What is the Project?

Birla Blitz is a project that turns NASA’s satellite images of Earth into sound, sends that sound through the air like a bird chirp, and lets a mobile phone hear it, decode it, and speak the explanation out loud.

It connects a computer and a mobile phone without using Wi-Fi, mobile data, Bluetooth, cables, or expensive cloud AI. The physical sound coming from the laptop speaker is the only bridge needed.

2. The Problem NASA Highlighted (Why Sight-Only Excludes People)

NASA collects incredible data about Earth—like heatwaves, windstorms, rain clouds, and humidity. However, NASA almost always shows this data as colorful visual maps and videos.

This creates a major problem:

  • Blind and low-vision individuals cannot see these images. If climate change and weather data are only shown through colors on a screen, millions of visually impaired people are left in the dark.
  • In addition, during real disasters like floods or cyclones, internet cables and cell towers often break down, making standard visual websites unreachable.

3. How the Project Works (Step-by-Step)

[1. Laptop: Reads Image] ──> [2. Makes Sound Chirp] ──> [3. Travels Through Air]

──> [4. Phone Hears It] ──> [5. Phone Reads & Speaks Aloud]

  1. Step 1: Inspecting the Image (On the Laptop)
    You drop a NASA satellite image or video into our website. The tool scans the pixels and reads the data (for example, detecting freezing cold −40∘C-40^\circ\text{C}−40∘C in polar areas or severe +48∘C+48^\circ\text{C}+48∘C heatwaves in the desert).
  2. Step 2: Converting Data into Sound (The Chirp)
    Instead of sending data over Wi-Fi, our built-in audio engine converts the data into a rapid, unique sound chirp (lasting less than 1 second) and plays it through the laptop speaker.
  3. Step 3: Traveling Through the Air
    The sound wave moves through the room air. There are no radio signals, passwords, or pairing steps.
  4. Step 4: Listening on the Phone
    Our small Android app (which needs zero internet) listens through the phone’s microphone. It catches the sound waves, figures out the frequencies, and understands the message.
  5. Step 5: Display & Automatic Voice Narration
    The phone instantly opens the satellite map and automatically reads the entire scientific explanation out loud using the phone's built-in voice.

4. How It Specifically Helps Blind and Low-Vision People

  • Turning Colors into Spoken Understanding:
    A blind person cannot see that a map has turned dark red or purple. Our app bridges this gap by describing the exact scientific meaning in plain speech.
  • Built-in Voice Without Extra Screen Readers:
    The user does not need to swipe around or fiddle with complicated controls. The moment the sound chirp is received, the phone’s native speaker automatically reads the observation aloud.
  • Multi-Sensory Feedback (Touch & Sound):
    The phone vibrates gently when the data arrives (haptic feedback) and plays an audio tone, so users know by touch and hearing that new data has been received.
  • High-Contrast Mode for Low-Vision Users:
    For users with partial vision, the app provides a high-contrast mode with bold white text, pure black backgrounds, and bright yellow borders, making it easy to read.

5. Why Is It Beneficial? (Key Advantages)

  1. 100% Offline (Works in Disasters):
    If a hurricane destroys local cell towers and the internet is down, an emergency radio or public loudspeaker can play this acoustic sound burst, and any nearby smartphone can receive the weather map and safety warnings.
  2. Zero Cost & Zero Subscriptions:
    We do not use paid cloud AI services (like OpenAI or ElevenLabs). It uses the phone’s own built-in speech engine, meaning it costs $0.00 forever and has zero delay.
  3. Universally Accessible Hardware:
    Every mobile phone made in the last 20 years has a microphone and a speaker. No special sensors, dongles, or expensive gadgets are required.
  4. Private and Secure:
    Because the data travels only through sound waves in the room and never touches the internet, it cannot be hacked or tracked remotely.
